# Example 8: Food chemistry stability Makefile
# Demonstrates a shelf-life workflow with sampling plan, assay data, and conclusions.

SHELL := /bin/bash
.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -o pipefail -c
.ONESHELL:
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help

PROJECT := vitamin-c-stability
PRODUCT ?= beverage-x
METHOD ?= hplc
STORAGE ?= 25C_60RH
TIMEPOINTS := d0 d7 d14 d28 d56
RAW := raw
PLAN := plan
DATA := data
ANALYSIS := analysis
REPORT := report
LOG := log

FILES_RAW := $(addprefix $(RAW)/,$(addsuffix .csv,$(TIMEPOINTS)))
FILES_DATA := $(addprefix $(DATA)/,$(addsuffix _assay.csv,$(TIMEPOINTS)))

.PHONY: help all init schedule sample assay analyze conclude clean distclean

help: ## Show food chemistry workflow targets
	@awk 'BEGIN{FS=":.*## "} /^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-]+:.*## / {printf "%-12s %s\n", $$1, $$2}' $(MAKEFILE_LIST)

all: init schedule sample assay analyze conclude ## Execute stability program

init: ## Initialize stability directories
	mkdir -p $(RAW) $(PLAN) $(DATA) $(ANALYSIS) $(REPORT) $(LOG)
	printf 'project=%s\nproduct=%s\nmethod=%s\nstorage=%s\n' '$(PROJECT)' '$(PRODUCT)' '$(METHOD)' '$(STORAGE)' > $(LOG)/context.env

schedule: $(PLAN)/sampling.tsv ## Build stability sampling schedule

$(PLAN)/sampling.tsv: | init
	printf 'timepoint\tstorage\tassay\n' > $@
	for t in $(TIMEPOINTS); do printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$$t" "$(STORAGE)" "$(METHOD)" >> $@; done

sample: $(FILES_RAW) ## Register raw chromatography files

$(RAW)/%.csv: | init
	printf 'retention_min,area\n' > $@
	for p in 1 2 3; do printf '5.%s,%s\n' "$$p" "$$((5000 + RANDOM % 2000))" >> $@; done

assay: $(FILES_DATA) $(DATA)/potency.csv ## Convert peak area to assay values

$(DATA)/%_assay.csv: $(RAW)/%.csv | init
	printf 'replicate,potency_pct_label\n' > $@
	awk -F, 'NR>1 {printf "%d,%.2f\n", NR-1, $$2/70}' $< >> $@

$(DATA)/potency.csv: $(FILES_DATA) | init
	printf 'timepoint,mean_potency_pct_label\n' > $@
	for f in $(FILES_DATA); do
		t=$$(basename $$f _assay.csv)
		m=$$(awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$$2;n++} END {if(n) printf "%.2f", s/n; else print "0.00"}' $$f)
		printf '%s,%s\n' "$$t" "$$m" >> $@
	done

analyze: $(ANALYSIS)/trend.tsv $(ANALYSIS)/spec.tsv ## Evaluate stability trend against specification

$(ANALYSIS)/trend.tsv: $(DATA)/potency.csv | init
	printf 'timepoint\tmean_potency\ttrend\n' > $@
	awk -F, 'NR>1 {trend=($$2+0>=90)?"within-trend":"declining"; printf "%s\t%s\t%s\n", $$1, $$2, trend}' $< >> $@

$(ANALYSIS)/spec.tsv: $(DATA)/potency.csv | init
	printf 'timepoint\tstatus\n' > $@
	awk -F, 'NR>1 {status=($$2+0>=85)?"PASS":"FAIL"; printf "%s\t%s\n", $$1, status}' $< >> $@

conclude: $(REPORT)/summary.md $(REPORT)/qc.txt ## Build shelf-life conclusion report

$(REPORT)/summary.md: $(PLAN)/sampling.tsv $(DATA)/potency.csv $(ANALYSIS)/trend.tsv $(ANALYSIS)/spec.tsv | init
	{
		echo "# Food Chemistry Stability Summary"
		echo
		echo "Product: $(PRODUCT)"
		echo "Method: $(METHOD)"
		echo "Storage: $(STORAGE)"
		echo
		echo "## Sampling Plan"
		cat $(PLAN)/sampling.tsv
		echo
		echo "## Potency"
		cat $(DATA)/potency.csv
		echo
		echo "## Trend"
		cat $(ANALYSIS)/trend.tsv
		echo
		echo "## Specification"
		cat $(ANALYSIS)/spec.tsv
	} > $@

$(REPORT)/qc.txt: $(FILES_RAW) $(FILES_DATA) | init
	{
		echo "QC"
		for f in $(FILES_RAW) $(FILES_DATA); do
			if [[ -s $$f ]]; then echo "OK $$f"; else echo "FAIL $$f"; fi
		done
	} > $@

method-check: ## Validate selected assay method
	@if [[ "$(METHOD)" != "hplc" && "$(METHOD)" != "titration" ]]; then \
		echo "Unsupported METHOD=$(METHOD)"; exit 1; \
	fi
	@echo "METHOD=$(METHOD) accepted"

show-timepoints: ## List scheduled timepoints
	@for t in $(TIMEPOINTS); do echo $$t; done

clean: ## Remove analytical outputs and reports
	rm -rf $(DATA)/* $(ANALYSIS)/* $(REPORT)/*

distclean: clean ## Remove all generated stability records
	rm -rf $(RAW)/* $(PLAN)/* $(LOG)/*

text:
# Example 9: Electrochemistry Makefile
# Best-practice pipeline for cyclic voltammetry processing and summary reporting.

SHELL := /bin/bash
.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -o pipefail -c
.ONESHELL:
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help

PROJECT := cv-screen
ELECTROLYTE ?= 0.1M-TBAPF6
SOLVENT ?= acetonitrile
REFERENCE ?= Ag/AgCl
SCAN_RATES := 50 100 200 500
SAMPLES := analyte_a analyte_b analyte_c ferrocene_blank
RAW := raw
PROC := processed
FIG := figures
REP := reports
LOG := log

RAW_TXT := $(foreach S,$(SAMPLES),$(foreach R,$(SCAN_RATES),$(RAW)/$(S)_$(R).txt))
PROC_CSV := $(foreach S,$(SAMPLES),$(foreach R,$(SCAN_RATES),$(PROC)/$(S)_$(R).csv))

.PHONY: help all init acquire process summarize figures report clean distclean

help: ## Print electrochemistry targets
	@awk 'BEGIN{FS=":.*## "} /^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-]+:.*## / {printf "%-12s %s\n", $$1, $$2}' $(MAKEFILE_LIST)

all: init acquire process summarize figures report ## Run cyclic voltammetry workflow

init: ## Initialize directory structure
	mkdir -p $(RAW) $(PROC) $(FIG) $(REP) $(LOG)
	printf 'project=%s\nelectrolyte=%s\nsolvent=%s\nreference=%s\n' '$(PROJECT)' '$(ELECTROLYTE)' '$(SOLVENT)' '$(REFERENCE)' > $(LOG)/setup.env

acquire: $(RAW_TXT) $(RAW)/manifest.tsv ## Stage raw voltammograms

$(RAW)/%.txt: | init
	printf 'potential_V,current_uA\n' > $@
	for p in -500 -250 0 250 500; do printf '%.3f,%s\n' "$$(awk 'BEGIN{printf '"$$p"'/1000}')" "$$(( -20 + RANDOM % 40 ))" >> $@; done

$(RAW)/manifest.tsv: $(RAW_TXT) | init
	printf 'file\n' > $@
	for f in $(RAW_TXT); do printf '%s\n' "$$f" >> $@; done

process: $(PROC_CSV) $(PROC)/peaks.csv ## Convert and extract peak features

$(PROC)/%.csv: $(RAW)/%.txt | init
	cp $< $@

$(PROC)/peaks.csv: $(PROC_CSV) | init
	printf 'sample,scan_rate_mV_s,e_pa_v,e_pc_v,i_pa_uA,i_pc_uA\n' > $@
	for s in $(SAMPLES); do
		for r in $(SCAN_RATES); do
			printf '%s,%s,0.32,0.11,%s,%s\n' "$$s" "$$r" "$$((10 + RANDOM % 40))" "$$((-1 * (10 + RANDOM % 30)))" >> $@
		done
	done

summarize: $(PROC)/summary.tsv ## Summarize electrochemical response by sample

$(PROC)/summary.tsv: $(PROC)/peaks.csv | init
	printf 'sample\tn_scans\n' > $@
	for s in $(SAMPLES); do
		n=$$(awk -F, -v s="$$s" 'NR>1 && $$1==s {n++} END {print n+0}' $<)
		printf '%s\t%s\n' "$$s" "$$n" >> $@
	done

figures: $(FIG)/overview.png $(FIG)/scan-rate.txt ## Create figure placeholders

$(FIG)/overview.png: $(PROC)/peaks.csv | init
	printf 'CV overview figure\n' > $@
	cat $< >> $@

$(FIG)/scan-rate.txt: $(PROC)/summary.tsv | init
	printf 'Scan-rate behavior summary\n' > $@
	cat $< >> $@

report: $(REP)/cv.md $(REP)/qc.txt ## Build electrochemistry report

$(REP)/cv.md: $(RAW)/manifest.tsv $(PROC)/peaks.csv $(PROC)/summary.tsv | init
	{
		echo "# Cyclic Voltammetry Report"
		echo
		echo "Electrolyte: $(ELECTROLYTE)"
		echo "Solvent: $(SOLVENT)"
		echo "Reference: $(REFERENCE)"
		echo
		echo "## Raw Files"
		cat $(RAW)/manifest.tsv
		echo
		echo "## Peak Table"
		cat $(PROC)/peaks.csv
		echo
		echo "## Summary"
		cat $(PROC)/summary.tsv
	} > $@

$(REP)/qc.txt: $(RAW_TXT) $(PROC_CSV) $(FIG)/overview.png | init
	{
		echo "QC"
		for f in $(RAW_TXT) $(PROC_CSV) $(FIG)/overview.png; do
			if [[ -s $$f ]]; then echo "OK $$f"; else echo "FAIL $$f"; fi
		done
	} > $@

params: ## Print experiment settings
	@echo "ELECTROLYTE=$(ELECTROLYTE)"
	@echo "SOLVENT=$(SOLVENT)"
	@echo "REFERENCE=$(REFERENCE)"

clean: ## Remove processed data, figures, and reports
	rm -rf $(PROC)/* $(FIG)/* $(REP)/*

distclean: clean ## Remove all generated electrochemistry files
	rm -rf $(RAW)/* $(LOG)/*

# Example 10: General laboratory chemistry QA Makefile
# Combines sample intake, method assignment, analysis, auditing, and release.

SHELL := /bin/bash
.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -o pipefail -c
.ONESHELL:
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help

LAB := central-chem
WORKLIST ?= WL-2026-04
REVIEWER ?= qa-lead
METHODS := gc hplc uvvis ic
SAMPLES := lot01 lot02 lot03 lot04 control_blank control_std
RAW := intake
PLAN := methods
DATA := measurements
OUT := output
AUDIT := audit
LOG := log

METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS := $(PLAN)/assignments.tsv
RAW_FILES := $(addprefix $(RAW)/,$(addsuffix .json,$(SAMPLES)))
DATA_FILES := $(addprefix $(DATA)/,$(addsuffix .csv,$(SAMPLES)))

.PHONY: help all init intake assign analyze verify release clean distclean

help: ## Show QA workflow targets
	@awk 'BEGIN{FS=":.*## "} /^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-]+:.*## / {printf "%-12s %s\n", $$1, $$2}' $(MAKEFILE_LIST)

all: init intake assign analyze verify release ## Complete chemistry QA workflow

init: ## Initialize directories and metadata
	mkdir -p $(RAW) $(PLAN) $(DATA) $(OUT) $(AUDIT) $(LOG)
	printf 'lab=%s\nworklist=%s\nreviewer=%s\n' '$(LAB)' '$(WORKLIST)' '$(REVIEWER)' > $(LOG)/context.env
	printf 'timestamp=%s\n' "$$(date -Is)" >> $(LOG)/context.env

intake: $(RAW_FILES) $(RAW)/manifest.tsv ## Register incoming chemistry samples

$(RAW)/%.json: | init
	cat > $@ <<EOF
{
  "sample": "$*",
  "received": true,
  "condition": "ambient",
  "priority": "routine"
}
EOF

$(RAW)/manifest.tsv: $(RAW_FILES) | init
	printf 'sample\tfile\n' > $@
	for s in $(SAMPLES); do printf '%s\t%s\n' "$$s" "$(RAW)/$$s.json" >> $@; done

assign: $(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS) ## Assign methods to samples

$(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS): $(RAW)/manifest.tsv | init
	printf 'sample\tmethod\n' > $@
	idx=0
	methods="$(METHODS)"
	for s in $(SAMPLES); do
		set -- $(METHODS)
		case $$idx in
			0) m=gc ;;
			1) m=hplc ;;
			2) m=uvvis ;;
			3) m=ic ;;
			*) m=hplc ;;
		esac
		printf '%s\t%s\n' "$$s" "$$m" >> $@
		idx=$$((idx+1))
	done

analyze: $(DATA_FILES) $(DATA)/summary.csv ## Produce mock measurements

$(DATA)/%.csv: $(RAW)/%.json $(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS) | init
	printf 'metric,value\n' > $@
	printf 'purity_pct,%s\n' "$$((90 + RANDOM % 10))" >> $@
	printf 'identity_match,%s\n' "pass" >> $@
	printf 'water_pct,0.%s\n' "$$((RANDOM % 9))" >> $@

$(DATA)/summary.csv: $(DATA_FILES) | init
	printf 'sample,purity_pct,identity_match,water_pct\n' > $@
	for s in $(SAMPLES); do
		purity=$$(awk -F, '$$1=="purity_pct" {print $$2}' $(DATA)/$$s.csv)
		identity=$$(awk -F, '$$1=="identity_match" {print $$2}' $(DATA)/$$s.csv)
		water=$$(awk -F, '$$1=="water_pct" {print $$2}' $(DATA)/$$s.csv)
		printf '%s,%s,%s,%s\n' "$$s" "$$purity" "$$identity" "$$water" >> $@
	done

verify: $(AUDIT)/checks.txt $(AUDIT)/disposition.tsv ## Audit outputs and determine sample disposition

$(AUDIT)/checks.txt: $(RAW_FILES) $(DATA_FILES) $(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS) | init
	{
		echo "Audit checks for $(WORKLIST)"
		for f in $(RAW_FILES) $(DATA_FILES) $(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS); do
			if [[ -s $$f ]]; then echo "OK $$f"; else echo "FAIL $$f"; fi
		done
	} > $@

$(AUDIT)/disposition.tsv: $(DATA)/summary.csv | init
	printf 'sample\tdisposition\n' > $@
	awk -F, 'NR>1 {d=($$2+0>=95 && $$3=="pass")?"release":"review"; printf "%s\t%s\n", $$1, d}' $< >> $@

release: $(OUT)/certificate.md $(OUT)/release.tsv ## Create release artifacts

$(OUT)/certificate.md: $(RAW)/manifest.tsv $(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS) $(DATA)/summary.csv $(AUDIT)/disposition.tsv | init
	{
		echo "# Chemistry QA Certificate"
		echo
		echo "Lab: $(LAB)"
		echo "Worklist: $(WORKLIST)"
		echo "Reviewer: $(REVIEWER)"
		echo
		echo "## Intake"
		cat $(RAW)/manifest.tsv
		echo
		echo "## Methods"
		cat $(METHOD_ASSIGNMENTS)
		echo
		echo "## Results"
		cat $(DATA)/summary.csv
		echo
		echo "## Disposition"
		cat $(AUDIT)/disposition.tsv
	} > $@

$(OUT)/release.tsv: $(AUDIT)/disposition.tsv | init
	cp $< $@

methods: ## Print available analytical methods
	@for m in $(METHODS); do echo $$m; done

reviewer-check: ## Ensure reviewer is set
	@if [[ -z "$(REVIEWER)" ]]; then echo "REVIEWER required"; exit 1; fi
	@echo "reviewer=$(REVIEWER)"

clean: ## Remove generated data, outputs, and audits
	rm -rf $(DATA)/* $(OUT)/* $(AUDIT)/*

distclean: clean ## Remove all generated QA records
	rm -rf $(RAW)/* $(PLAN)/* $(LOG)/*

  </Description>
  <Materials>
    <Material>
      <Name>Salicylic Acid</Name>
      <Quantity>5.0 grams</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Acetic Anhydride</Name>
      <Quantity>10.0 mL</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Sodium Hydroxide</Name>
      <Quantity>1.0 gram</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Distilled Water</Name>
      <Quantity>50.0 mL</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Ice Bath</Name>
      <Quantity>As needed</Quantity>
    </Material>
  </Materials>
  <Procedure>
    <Step number="1">
      <Description>Dissolve 5.0 grams of salicylic acid in 20.0 mL of distilled water in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="2">
      <Description>Add 1.0 gram of sodium hydroxide to the flask and stir until the salicylic acid is completely dissolved.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="3">
      <Description>Slowly add 10.0 mL of acetic anhydride to the flask while stirring and cooling the mixture in an ice bath.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="4">
      <Description>Continue stirring the mixture for an additional 15 minutes to ensure complete reaction.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="5">
      <Description>Transfer the mixture to a separatory funnel and wash it with 20.0 mL of distilled water to remove any remaining sodium acetate.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="6">
      <Description>Dry the organic layer with anhydrous sodium sulfate and filter the mixture to remove any solid impurities.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="7">
      <Description>Evaporate the solvent from the filtered mixture using a rotary evaporator to obtain the crude aspirin.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="8">
      <Description>Recrystallize the crude aspirin from hot water to obtain pure aspirin.</Description>
    </Step>
  </Procedure>

  <Description>

  </Description>
  <Materials>
    <Material>
      <Name>Benzene</Name>

    </Material>

      <Name>Unknown Solute (e.g., Sucrose or Urea)</Name>

    <Step number="6">

    </Step>

<ChemistryExperiment>
  <Title>Synthesis of Esters from Carboxylic Acids and Alcohols</Title>
  <Description>
    This experiment demonstrates the synthesis of esters from carboxylic acids and alcohols using an acid-catalyzed esterification reaction.
  </Description>
  <Materials>
    <Material>
      <Name>Ethanoic Acid (Acetic Acid)</Name>
      <Quantity>10.0 mL</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Ethanol</Name>
      <Quantity>10.0 mL</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4)</Name>
      <Quantity>1.0 mL</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Distilled Water</Name>
      <Quantity>50.0 mL</Quantity>
    </Material>
    <Material>
      <Name>Separatory Funnel</Name>
      <Quantity>1</Quantity>
    </Material>
  </Materials>
  <Procedure>
    <Step number="1">
      <Description>Add 10.0 mL of ethanoic acid and 10.0 mL of ethanol to a separatory funnel.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="2">
      <Description>Add 1.0 mL of sulfuric acid to the separatory funnel as a catalyst and shake the mixture.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="3">
      <Description>Allow the mixture to react for 1-2 hours at room temperature.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="4">
      <Description>Add 50.0 mL of distilled water to the separatory funnel and shake to extract the ester product.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="5">
      <Description>Allow the mixture to separate into two layers, with the organic layer (ester) on top.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="6">
      <Description>Remove the organic layer and dry it with anhydrous sodium sulfate.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="7">
      <Description>Evaporate the solvent from the organic layer using a rotary evaporator to obtain the crude ester product.</Description>
    </Step>
    <Step number="8">
      <Description>Determine the boiling point of the ester to confirm the product's purity.</Description>
    </Step>
  </Procedure>
  <Results>
    <Description>
      The experiment should yield approximately 15.0 mL of ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate) with a boiling point of 77°C.
    </Description>
  </Results>

  <title>Protein Crystallization Screening</title>
  <objective>Identify initial crystallization conditions for recombinant lysozyme</objective>
  <materials>
    <protein>
      <name>Hen Egg White Lysozyme</name>
      <concentration>50 mg/mL</concentration>
      <buffer>0.1 M sodium acetate, pH 4.5</buffer>
      <storage>−80 °C in 50 μL aliquots</storage>
    </protein>
    <screen>
      <name>Hampton Research Crystal Screen</name>
      <lot>CS-2023-045</lot>
      <storage>4 °C</storage>
    </screen>
  </materials>
  <equipment>
    <item>24-well sitting drop plates (Hampton Research)</item>
    <item>Siliconized glass coverslips</item>
    <item>Microscope with 10× objective</item>
    <item>Temperature-controlled incubator (18 °C)</item>
  </equipment>
  <procedure>
    <step>
      <number>1</number>
      <action>Thaw protein aliquot on ice (30 min)</action>
    </step>
    <step>
      <number>2</number>
      <action>Pipette 1 μL protein solution onto coverslip</action>
      <note>Use positive displacement pipette for accuracy</note>
    </step>
    <step>
      <number>3</number>
      <action>Add 1 μL reservoir solution from well A1</action>

    <step>
      <number>4</number>

<!DOCTYPE teaching SYSTEM "teaching.dtd">
<chemistry-lesson>
  <topic>Acid-Base Titration Curves</topic>
  <level>Undergraduate analytical chemistry</level>
  <learning-objectives>
    <objective>Calculate pH at different points in strong acid-strong base titration</objective>
    <objective>Identify equivalence point from titration curve</objective>
    <objective>Select appropriate indicator based on pH transition range</objective>
  </learning-objectives>
  <experiment>
    <title>Titration of HCl with NaOH</title>
    <materials>
      <item>0.1 M HCl (standardized)</item>
      <item>0.1 M NaOH (to be standardized)</item>
      <item>Phenolphthalein indicator</item>
      <item>pH meter (calibrated at pH 4, 7, 10)</item>
    </materials>
    <data-collection>
      <measurement>
        <volume>0.0 mL NaOH</volume>
        <ph>1.0</ph>
      </measurement>
      <measurement>
        <volume>24.9 mL NaOH</volume>
        <ph>3.9</ph>
      </measurement>
      <measurement>
        <volume>25.0 mL NaOH</volume>
        <ph>7.0</ph>
        <note>Equivalence point</note>
      </measurement>
    </data-collection>
  </experiment>
  <calculations>
    <step>
      <description>Initial pH of 0.1 M HCl</description>
      <equation>pH = -log[H⁺] = -log(0.1) = 1.0</equation>
    </step>
    <step>
      <description>pH before equivalence point (after 24.9 mL NaOH)</description>
      <equation>[H⁺] = (moles H⁺ remaining) / (total volume)</equation>
      <equation>[H⁺] = (0.0025 - 0.00249) / 0.0499 = 2.0×10⁻⁴ M</equation>
      <equation>pH = 3.7 (experimental: 3.9)</equation>
    </step>
  </calculations>
  <assessment>
    <question>Why does phenolphthalein (pH range 8.2-10.0) work for this titration?</question>
    <answer>The pH jump at equivalence point (4-10) includes phenolphthalein's range</answer>
  </assessment>
  <safety>
    <note>Wear eye protection when handling acids and bases</note>
    <note>Dispose of neutralized waste in appropriate container</note>
  </safety>
</chemistry-lesson>

text: Biology is the natural science that studies life and living organisms, including their physical structure, chemical processes, molecular interactions, physiological mechanisms, development, and evolution. Despite the complexity of the science, certain unifying concepts consolidate it into a single, coherent field. Biology recognizes the cell as the basic unit of life, genes as the basic unit of heredity, and evolution as the engine that propels the synthesis and creation of new species. Living organisms are open systems that survive by transforming energy and decreasing their local entropy to maintain a stable, vital condition. Sub-disciplines of biology are recognized on the basis of the scale at which life is studied and the methods used to study it. Biochemistry examines the rudimentary chemistry of life; molecular biology studies the complex interactions of biological macromolecules; cellular biology examines the basic building block of all life, the cell; physiology examines the physical and chemical functions of tissues, organs, and organ systems of an organism; and ecology examines how organisms interact in their environment.

text: The cell is the basic structural, functional, and biological unit of all known organisms. A cell is the smallest unit of life. Cells consist of cytoplasm enclosed within a membrane, which contains many biomolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids. Organisms can be unicellular (consisting of a single cell; e.g., bacteria) or multicellular (including plants and animals). While the number of cells in plants and animals varies, humans contain some 100 trillion cells. The study of cells is called cell biology. Prokaryotic cells are single-celled organisms that lack a cell nucleus, and other membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells are organisms whose cells have a nucleus enclosed within a nuclear envelope. The nucleus contains the cell's genetic material. Eukaryotic cells are typically much larger than prokaryotic cells and have a variety of internal membranes and structures, called organelles, and a cytoskeleton.

text: Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation, and heredity in living organisms. It is generally considered a field of biology, but intersects frequently with many other life sciences and is strongly linked with the study of information systems. The father of genetics is Gregor Mendel, a Moravian Augustinian friar who studied inheritance patterns in pea plants in the mid-19th century. Mendel observed that organisms inherit traits through discrete units of inheritance, which are now called genes. Genes are sequences of DNA or RNA that code for a molecule (usually a protein) that has a function. The full set of genes in an organism is called its genome. Genes can be passed down from parent to offspring, meaning traits can be inherited. Genetic variation refers to differences in the DNA sequence among individuals or populations. This variation is key for evolution, as it provides the raw material for natural selection.

text: Evolution is the change in the heritable characteristics of biological populations over successive generations. These characteristics are the expressions of genes that are passed on from parent to offspring during reproduction. Different characteristics tend to exist within any given population as a result of mutation, genetic recombination, and other sources of genetic variation. Evolution occurs when these heritable differences become more common or rare in a population, either non-randomly through natural selection and sexual selection or randomly through genetic drift. Natural selection is the process where organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring. This leads to an increase in the frequency of advantageous traits in a population over time. The primary mechanisms that drive evolution are natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, and mutation. The study of evolution provides a framework for understanding the diversity of life on Earth.

text: Ecology is the scientific study of the interactions among organisms and their biophysical environment, which includes both biotic and abiotic components. The field of ecology is often taught in terms of levels of organization: organism, population, community, ecosystem, and biosphere. An ecosystem consists of all the organisms and the physical environment with which they interact. Ecosystems are dynamic entities that contain both living parts (biotic components) and non-living parts (abiotic components) that interact as a unit. Examples of biotic components include plants, animals, and microorganisms, while abiotic components include sunlight, water, temperature, and soil. Ecological processes, such as primary production, decomposition, and nutrient cycling, regulate the flux of energy and matter through an ecosystem. Human activities have a significant impact on ecosystems, leading to concerns about biodiversity loss and climate change.

text: Photosynthesis is a process used by plants and other organisms to convert light energy into chemical energy that can later be released to fuel the organisms' activities (energy transformation). This chemical energy is stored in carbohydrate molecules, such as sugars, which are synthesized from carbon dioxide and water. Most plants, algae, and cyanobacteria perform photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is largely responsible for producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and supplies most of the energy necessary for life on Earth. The primary pigment involved in photosynthesis is chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy. The process occurs in two main stages: the light-dependent reactions and the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle). The light-dependent reactions convert light energy into chemical energy in the form of ATP and NADPH, while the Calvin cycle uses these energy carriers to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.

text: The human body is the entire structure of a human being. It is composed of many different types of cells that together create tissues and subsequently organ systems. They comprise a variety of biological systems that maintain homeostasis and ensure survival. These systems include the circulatory system, respiratory system, digestive system, nervous system, endocrine system, immune system, integumentary system, skeletal system, muscular system, and reproductive system. Each system has specific functions that contribute to the overall well-being of the body. For example, the circulatory system transports blood, oxygen, nutrients, and hormones throughout the body, while the nervous system is responsible for communication and coordination. The study of the human body involves anatomy (the study of structure) and physiology (the study of function). Understanding these systems is crucial for medicine and healthcare.

text: Viruses are microscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside the living cells of an organism. Viruses can infect all types of life forms, from animals and plants to microorganisms, including bacteria and archaea. Since Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 article describing a non-bacterial pathogen infecting tobacco plants and the discovery of the tobacco mosaic virus by Martinus Beijerinck in 1898, more than 9,000 virus species have been described in detail out of the millions of types of viruses in the environment. Viruses are found in almost every ecosystem on Earth and are the most numerous biological entities. A complete virus particle, known as a virion, consists of genetic material (either DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protective protein coat called a capsid. Viruses lack the cellular machinery to replicate on their own and must hijack the host cell's machinery to produce new virions. This parasitic nature makes them significant pathogens causing diseases in various organisms.

text: Biotechnology is the technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives thereof, to make or modify products or processes for a specific use. Depending on the tools and applications, it often overlaps with the fields of bioengineering, biomedical engineering, biomanufacturing, molecular engineering, molecular biology, and many others. For thousands of years, humankind has used biotechnology (e.g., in brewing beer and bread making). Modern biotechnology, however, often refers to the use of genetic engineering and cell culture technologies. Key applications include the development of genetically modified crops, the production of pharmaceuticals like insulin and vaccines, gene therapy for genetic disorders, and the creation of diagnostic tools. Biotechnology holds immense potential for addressing global challenges in health, agriculture, and environmental sustainability.

text: Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system. It is a multidisciplinary science that combines physiology, anatomy, molecular biology, developmental biology, cytology, computer science, and mathematical modeling to understand the fundamental and emergent properties of neurons and neural circuits. The scope of neuroscience has broadened to include different approaches used to study the nervous system at different scales. The techniques used by neuroscientists have also expanded enormously, from molecular and cellular studies of individual neurons to imaging of sensory, motor, and cognitive tasks in the brain. The field has advanced significantly in understanding how the brain functions, from basic sensory perception to complex cognitive processes like memory and decision-making. Neurological disorders and mental health conditions are also major areas of research within neuroscience, aiming to develop new treatments and therapies.

text: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms, encompassing their structure, function, growth, evolution, and distribution. At its core, biology explores the complexity of life at multiple levels, from molecular interactions within cells to the dynamics of ecosystems. One fundamental concept is the cell theory, which states that all living things are composed of cells, the basic unit of life. Cells themselves are intricate systems, containing organelles like the nucleus (housing DNA), mitochondria (energy production), and ribosomes (protein synthesis). Cellular respiration, a process occurring in mitochondria, converts glucose into ATP, the energy currency of the cell. Photosynthesis in plant chloroplasts similarly transforms sunlight into chemical energy, sustaining most life on Earth. Genetic information is encoded in DNA, which undergoes replication during cell division via mitosis or meiosis. Mutations in DNA drive genetic diversity, a cornerstone of evolution through natural selection, as proposed by Darwin. Organisms adapt to their environment over generations, with advantageous traits becoming more prevalent. Ecosystems illustrate the interdependence of species and abiotic factors; food webs depict energy flow from producers to decomposers. Biodiversity, shaped by speciation and extinction, is critical for ecosystem resilience. Human biology integrates anatomy, physiology, and genetics, with advancements like CRISPR enabling gene editing. Conservation biology addresses threats like habitat loss, aiming to preserve species and ecological balance. Emerging fields like synthetic biology merge biology with engineering, creating organisms with novel functions. From microscopic bacteria to towering sequoias, biology unravels the mechanisms sustaining life in all its forms.

text: The human body is a marvel of biological engineering, composed of organ systems working in harmony. The circulatory system, driven by the heart, transports oxygen, nutrients, and hormones via blood vessels. Blood, a liquid tissue, contains red blood cells (carrying hemoglobin), white blood cells (immune defense), and platelets (clotting). The respiratory system facilitates gas exchange: oxygen enters the bloodstream in the lungs, while carbon dioxide is expelled. Alveoli, tiny air sacs, maximize surface area for efficient diffusion. The digestive system breaks down food mechanically and chemically, starting in the mouth with salivary enzymes and ending in the intestines, where nutrients are absorbed. The liver produces bile, aiding fat digestion, while the pancreas releases insulin to regulate blood sugar. The nervous system, comprising the brain, spinal cord, and neurons, transmits electrical signals for rapid communication. Synapses relay neurotransmitters between nerve cells, enabling thought, movement, and sensation. Hormones from the endocrine system, like thyroid hormones or adrenaline, regulate metabolism and stress responses. The skeletal system provides structural support and protection, with bones like the femur (the longest bone) and ossicles (tiny ear bones). Muscles, attached to bones via tendons, contract to produce movement. The integumentary system—skin, hair, and nails—acts as a barrier against pathogens and regulates temperature. Immune cells like lymphocytes identify and destroy invaders, with vaccines harnessing memory cells for long-term protection. Homeostasis, maintained by feedback loops, ensures internal stability despite external changes. Disorders like diabetes or hypertension highlight the consequences of system imbalances, while medical advancements continue to enhance human health.

text: Ecology examines how organisms interact with their environment and each other. Populations, communities, and ecosystems form the hierarchy of ecological study. A population consists of individuals of the same species in a habitat; their growth is influenced by birth rates, death rates, and resource availability. Communities involve multiple populations coexisting, with interspecies relationships like predation (e.g., wolves hunting deer), competition (e.g., lions vs. hyenas), and mutualism (e.g., bees and flowers). Ecosystems integrate biotic factors (living organisms) with abiotic factors (sunlight, water, soil). Producers (plants), consumers (herbivores, carnivores), and decomposers (fungi, bacteria) form food chains that cycle energy and nutrients. Trophic levels illustrate energy transfer, with only ~10% efficiency between levels, limiting the length of food chains. Biomes, such as tropical rainforests or tundras, are large ecological regions defined by climate and vegetation. The carbon cycle involves photosynthesis absorbing CO2 and respiration releasing it, while the nitrogen cycle relies on bacteria to fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms. Human activities, like deforestation and fossil fuel combustion, disrupt these cycles, contributing to climate change and biodiversity loss. Conservation strategies, including protected areas and sustainable practices, aim to mitigate ecological degradation. Indicator species, such as amphibians sensitive to pollution, monitor environmental health. Understanding ecological principles is vital for addressing global challenges like habitat fragmentation and invasive species, ensuring the survival of Earth's interconnected life systems.

text: Genetics, the study of heredity, reveals how traits are passed from parents to offspring. Gregor Mendel's pea plant experiments established the laws of segregation and independent assortment, forming the basis of classical genetics. DNA, structured as a double helix, consists of nucleotides with four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G). Base pairing (A-T, C-G) ensures accurate replication during the S phase of the cell cycle. Genes, segments of DNA, code for proteins via transcription (mRNA synthesis) and translation (ribosome assembly of amino acids). Mutations, like point mutations or chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., Down syndrome), can alter gene function, sometimes causing diseases. Inheritance patterns include dominant/recessive (e.g., cystic fibrosis), codominant (blood types), and polygenic traits (height). Epigenetics explores heritable changes in gene expression without altering DNA sequence, such as DNA methylation. Biotechnology leverages genetic knowledge: PCR amplifies DNA, gel electrophoresis separates fragments, and CRISPR-Cas9 allows precise gene editing. GMOs (genetically modified organisms) are engineered for pest resistance or nutritional enhancement. Personalized medicine uses genetic profiling to tailor treatments, as in cancer therapies targeting specific mutations. Ethical debates surround genetic privacy, designer babies, and ecological impacts of gene drives. From Mendel's peas to the Human Genome Project, genetics continues to transform medicine, agriculture, and our understanding of life itself.

text: Evolution, the unifying theory of biology, explains the diversity of life through descent with modification. Charles Darwin's 1859 theory of natural selection posits that individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more, passing those traits to offspring. Evidence includes fossil records showing transitional forms (e.g., Archaeopteryx linking dinosaurs and birds), biogeography (Galápagos finches), and homologous structures (e.g., vertebrate limbs). Genetic variation arises from mutations, sexual reproduction, and gene flow. Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated, such as via geographic barriers or behavioral differences. Adaptive radiation, exemplified by Darwin's finches, results in multiple species from a common ancestor. Convergent evolution produces analogous structures (e.g., wings in bats and insects) in unrelated species facing similar pressures. Evolutionary developmental biology (evo-devo) highlights how changes in developmental genes (e.g., Hox genes) drive morphological diversity. Antibiotic resistance in bacteria and pesticide resistance in insects demonstrate evolution in action. Phylogenetic trees map evolutionary relationships using molecular data, like comparing DNA sequences. While evolution is often gradual, punctuated equilibrium suggests rapid changes during brief periods. Despite overwhelming evidence, misconceptions persist, such as equating evolution with 'progress' or dismissing it as 'just a theory.' Evolutionary principles underpin modern biology, from vaccine development to understanding human origins.

text: Microbiology delves into microscopic organisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists. Bacteria, prokaryotic cells, exhibit diverse shapes (cocci, bacilli, spirilla) and play critical roles in decomposition, nitrogen fixation, and human health. Some, like Escherichia coli, aid digestion, while others cause diseases (e.g., tuberculosis by Mycobacterium tuberculosis). Antibiotics target bacterial cells without harming humans, though resistance is a growing concern. Viruses, acellular entities, require host cells to replicate, causing illnesses like influenza or COVID-19. Vaccines stimulate immune memory against viral antigens. Fungi, such as Penicillium, produce antibiotics and decompose organic matter, while mycorrhizal fungi form symbiotic relationships with plant roots. Protists, a diverse group, include algae (photosynthetic) and pathogens like Plasmodium (malaria). Microbiomes, communities of microbes in environments like the human gut, influence immunity and metabolism. Extremophiles thrive in harsh conditions (e.g., thermophiles in hot springs), offering insights into life's origins and potential extraterrestrial life. Microbial biotechnology produces insulin via recombinant DNA, biofuels, and bioremediation solutions. Understanding microbiology is crucial for combating diseases, advancing industry, and sustaining ecosystems.

text: Botany, the study of plants, explores their physiology, structure, and ecological roles. Photosynthesis in chloroplasts converts light energy into glucose, releasing oxygen essential for most life. Plant cells have rigid cell walls made of cellulose, distinguishing them from animal cells. Vascular plants (e.g., ferns, trees) possess xylem (water transport) and phloem (nutrient transport), enabling terrestrial adaptation. Roots anchor plants and absorb water, while leaves optimize light capture via chlorophyll. Reproduction varies: nonvascular plants like mosses rely on moisture for fertilization, whereas angiosperms (flowering plants) use pollen and seeds. Flowers attract pollinators with colors and nectar, leading to seed formation in fruits. Gymnosperms, like pines, bear naked seeds in cones. Plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins) regulate growth, phototropism, and fruit ripening. Ethnobotany examines human-plant interactions, from medicinal herbs (e.g., aspirin from willow bark) to agriculture. Threats like deforestation and climate change endanger plant biodiversity, impacting carbon sequestration and habitats. Conservation efforts include seed banks and reforestation. Plants also inspire biomimicry, such as Velcro mimicking burrs. From algae to towering redwoods, botany illuminates the foundation of terrestrial ecosystems.

text: Zoology examines the diversity, behavior, and physiology of animals. Animals are multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes with specialized tissues. Invertebrates, lacking backbones, include arthropods (insects, spiders) with exoskeletons and metamorphosis, and mollusks (snails, octopuses) with radulas or tentacles. Chordates possess a notochord or backbone; vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) have endoskeletons and complex organ systems. Fish use gills for respiration and fins for locomotion, while amphibians (e.g., frogs) transition from aquatic larvae to terrestrial adults. Reptiles, with scaly skin and amniotic eggs, dominate arid environments. Birds evolved feathers and lightweight bones for flight, sharing ancestry with dinosaurs. Mammals, including humans, are distinguished by hair and milk production. Social behaviors, like wolf packs or bee colonies, enhance survival through cooperation. Migration, hibernation, and camouflage are adaptations to environmental challenges. Zoology informs conservation, as habitat destruction threatens species like tigers and coral reefs. Ethology, the study of animal behavior, reveals insights into intelligence, communication, and emotions. From microscopic rotifers to blue whales, zoology uncovers the marvels of animal life.

text: Biochemistry investigates the chemical processes sustaining life. Central to this is metabolism, the network of enzyme-catalyzed reactions breaking down (catabolism) or building up (anabolism) molecules. Glycolysis, occurring in the cytoplasm, splits glucose into pyruvate, generating ATP and NADH. The citric acid cycle in mitochondria further oxidizes pyruvate, producing electron carriers for the electron transport chain, which synthesizes most ATP. Enzymes, proteins that lower activation energy, are sensitive to temperature and pH; denaturation disrupts their active site. Coenzymes like NAD+ and ATP itself act as carriers in reactions. Lipids form cell membranes via phospholipid bilayers, while proteins serve structural, enzymatic, and signaling roles. Nucleic acids store genetic information, and carbohydrates provide quick energy. Hormones like insulin regulate metabolic pathways, and second messengers like cAMP relay signals. Biochemical techniques, including chromatography and spectrophotometry, analyze biomolecules. Disorders like phenylketonuria result from enzyme deficiencies, underscoring biochemistry's medical relevance. Advances in proteomics and metabolomics offer insights into disease mechanisms, paving the way for targeted therapies and biotechnological innovations.

text: Biotechnology harnesses biological systems to develop technologies and products. Recombinant DNA technology inserts genes into plasmids, enabling bacteria to produce human insulin. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies DNA for diagnostics, forensics, and research. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) include crops with pest resistance (Bt corn) or enhanced nutrients (Golden Rice). CRISPR-Cas9, a revolutionary gene-editing tool, uses guide RNA to target specific DNA sequences for modification, offering potential cures for genetic disorders. Synthetic biology designs artificial organisms with novel functions, such as bacteria that degrade pollutants. Stem cell therapy explores regenerative medicine, using pluripotent cells to repair damaged tissues. Bioinformatics combines biology with computational tools to analyze genomes, identifying disease-linked genes. Ethical concerns include gene patenting, ecological risks of GMOs, and the possibility of human germline editing. Biotechnology also impacts industry, producing biofuels, biodegradable plastics, and enzymes for manufacturing. Personalized medicine tailors treatments based on genetic profiles, improving efficacy and reducing side effects. As biotechnology evolves, balancing innovation with ethical stewardship remains critical to address global health, food security, and environmental challenges.

# Install security scanning tools

    trivy \
    && safety check --full-report

# Install chemical safety tools
RUN pip3 install --no-cache-dir \
    rdkit \
    pandas \
    numpy \
    scikit-learn \
    openpyxl \
    sqlalchemy \
    psycopg2-binary \
    && python3 -c "import rdkit; print(f'RDKit version: {rdkit.__version__}')"

# Download ChEMBL database
WORKDIR /data
RUN wget https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/chembl/ChEMBLdb/releases/chembl_${CHEMBL_VERSION}/chembl_${CHEMBL_VERSION}.zip \
    && echo "${CHEMBL_SHA256} chembl_${CHEMBL_VERSION}.zip" | sha256sum -c \
    && unzip chembl_${CHEMBL_VERSION}.zip \
    && rm chembl_${CHEMBL_VERSION}.zip

# Create compliance checking scripts
RUN mkdir -p /app/compliance
RUN echo '#!/usr/bin/env python3
import pandas as pd
import sqlite3
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import Descriptors
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def check_osha_compliance(smiles):
    """Check OSHA compliance for chemical"""
    mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smiles)
    if not mol:
        return {"error": "Invalid SMILES"}
    
    mw = Descriptors.MolWt(mol)
    logp = Descriptors.MolLogP(mol)
    tpsa = Descriptors.TPSA(mol)
    
    # OSHA compliance rules
    violations = []
    if mw > 500:
        violations.append("Molecular weight exceeds OSHA limits")
    if logp > 5:
        violations.append("LogP indicates high lipophilicity")
    if tpsa > 140:
        violations.append("Polar surface area exceeds limits")
    
    return {
        "molecular_weight": mw,
        "logp": logp,
        "tpsa": tpsa,
        "violations": violations,
        "compliant": len(violations) == 0
    }

def check_epa_compliance(smiles):
    """Check EPA compliance for chemical"""
    mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smiles)
    if not mol:
        return {"error": "Invalid SMILES"}
    
    # EPA rules based on functional groups
    violations = []
    
    # Check for banned groups
    banned_smarts = [
        "[CX4][Cl,Br,I]",  # Halogenated carbons
        "[#6][N+](=O)[O-]",  # Nitro groups
        "C=O",  # Carbonyl
    ]
    
    for smart in banned_smarts:
        pattern = Chem.MolFromSmarts(smart)
        if mol.HasSubstructMatch(pattern):
            violations.append(f"Contains {smart} group")
    
    return {
        "violations": violations,
        "compliant": len(violations) == 0
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Test with example
    test_smiles = "CC(=O)OC1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)O"  # Aspirin
    osha_result = check_osha_compliance(test_smiles)
    epa_result = check_epa_compliance(test_smiles)
    
    logger.info(f"OSHA Compliance: {osha_result}")
    logger.info(f"EPA Compliance: {epa_result}")' > /app/compliance/checker.py \
    && chmod +x /app/compliance/checker.py

# Create audit logging setup
RUN echo '#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
import datetime
import logging
from logging.handlers import RotatingFileHandler

# Setup audit logging
audit_logger = logging.getLogger("audit")
audit_logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

handler = RotatingFileHandler(
    "/var/log/chemical_audit.log",
    maxBytes=10485760,  # 10MB
    backupCount=5
)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(
    "%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
))
audit_logger.addHandler(handler)

def log_compliance_check(smiles, user, result):
    audit_logger.info(json.dumps({
        "timestamp": datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        "user": user,
        "smiles": smiles,
        "result": result,
        "action": "compliance_check"
    }))' > /app/compliance/audit.py \
    && chmod +x /app/compliance/audit.py

# Create non-root user
RUN groupadd -r safety && useradd -r -g safety safety \
    && chown -R safety:safety /app \
    && chown -R safety:safety /data \
    && mkdir -p /var/log \
    && chown safety:safety /var/log

WORKDIR /app
USER safety

VOLUME ["/var/log"]

CMD ["python3", "/app/compliance/checker.py"]

# Dockerfile for High-Throughput Screening with AutoDock Vina
# Best practices: parallel processing, job queueing, result aggregation

FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    git \
    wget \
    python3 \
    python3-pip \
    python3-dev \
    openmpi-bin \
    libopenmpi-dev \
    libboost-all-dev \
    libeigen3-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install AutoDock Vina
WORKDIR /tmp
RUN wget https://github.com/ccsb-scripps/AutoDock-Vina/archive/refs/tags/v1.2.3.tar.gz \
    && tar xzf v1.2.3.tar.gz \
    && rm v1.2.3.tar.gz \
    && cd AutoDock-Vina-1.2.3 \
    && mkdir build \
    && cd build \
    && cmake .. \
    && make -j$(nproc) \
    && make install \
    && cd /tmp \
    && rm -rf AutoDock-Vina-1.2.3

# Install Python packages for screening
RUN pip3 install --no-cache-dir \
    rdkit \
    pandas \
    numpy \
    scipy \
    scikit-learn \
    joblib \
    redis \
    celery \
    flower \
    sqlalchemy \
    psycopg2-binary \
    && python3 -c "import rdkit; print(f'RDKit installed: {rdkit.__version__}')"

# Create screening pipeline
RUN mkdir -p /app/screening \
    && mkdir -p /app/data/ligands \
    && mkdir -p /app/data/receptors \
    && mkdir -p /app/results \
    && mkdir -p /app/logs

# Create ligand preparation script
RUN echo '#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import sys
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem
import subprocess

def prepare_ligand(smiles, output_dir):
    """Convert SMILES to PDBQT format for Vina"""
    mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smiles)
    if not mol:
        return None
    
    # Add hydrogens
    mol = Chem.AddHs(mol)
    
    # Generate 3D coordinates
    AllChem.EmbedMolecule(mol)
    AllChem.UFFOptimizeMolecule(mol)
    
    # Save as PDB
    pdb_file = os.path.join(output_dir, "ligand.pdb")
    Chem.MolToPDBFile(mol, pdb_file)
    
    # Convert to PDBQT using Open Babel (would need openbabel installed)
    pdbqt_file = os.path.join(output_dir, "ligand.pdbqt")
    # In production, you would call: obabel -ipdb ligand.pdb -opdbqt -O ligand.pdbqt
    
    return pdbqt_file

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("Usage: python prepare_ligand.py <smiles> <output_dir>")
        sys.exit(1)
    
    smiles = sys.argv[1]
    output_dir = sys.argv[2]
    
    result = prepare_ligand(smiles, output_dir)
    print(f"Prepared ligand: {result}")' > /app/screening/prepare_ligand.py \
    && chmod +x /app/screening/prepare_ligand.py

# Create docking script
RUN echo '#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import subprocess
import json
import pandas as pd
from datetime import datetime

def run_docking(receptor_pdbqt, ligand_pdbqt, output_dir, config):
    """Run AutoDock Vina docking"""
    # Create configuration file
    config_file = os.path.join(output_dir, "config.txt")
    with open(config_file, "w") as f:
        f.write(f"receptor = {receptor_pdbqt}
")
        f.write(f"ligand = {ligand_pdbqt}
")
        f.write(f"center_x = {config["center_x"]}
")
        f.write(f"center_y = {config["center_y"]}
")
        f.write(f"center_z = {config["center_z"]}
")
        f.write(f"size_x = {config["size_x"]}
")
        f.write(f"size_y = {config["size_y"]}
")
        f.write(f"size_z = {config["size_z"]}
")
        f.write("exhaustiveness = 8
")
        f.write("num_modes = 10
")
    
    # Run Vina
    output_file = os.path.join(output_dir, "docking_results.pdbqt")
    log_file = os.path.join(output_dir, "docking.log")
    
    cmd = [
        "vina",
        "--config", config_file,
        "--out", output_file,
        "--log", log_file
    ]
    
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
    
    # Parse results
    scores = []
    with open(log_file, "r") as f:
        for line in f:
            if "REMARK VINA RESULT:" in line:
                parts = line.strip().split()
                scores.append(float(parts[3]))
    
    return {
        "output_file": output_file,
        "log_file": log_file,
        "scores": scores,
        "best_score": min(scores) if scores else None,
        "timestamp": datetime.now().isoformat()
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    config = {
        "center_x": 15.0,
        "center_y": 15.0,
        "center_z": 15.0,
        "size_x": 20.0,
        "size_y": 20.0,
        "size_z": 20.0
    }
    
    result = run_docking(
        "/app/data/receptors/receptor.pdbqt",
        "/app/data/ligands/ligand.pdbqt",
        "/app/results/test",
        config
    )
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))' > /app/screening/run_docking.py \
    && chmod +x /app/screening/run_docking.py

# Create job scheduler script
RUN echo '#!/usr/bin/env python3
from celery import Celery
import redis
import json

app = Celery(
    "screening",
    broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",
    backend="redis://localhost:6379/0"
)

@app.task
def screen_ligand(ligand_id, smiles, receptor_file):
    """Screen a single ligand against receptor"""
    # This would call prepare_ligand.py and run_docking.py
    # Return docking scores
    return {
        "ligand_id": ligand_id,
        "smiles": smiles,
        "best_score": -9.5,  # Example score
        "status": "completed"
    }

@app.task
def batch_screen(ligands_batch, receptor_file):
    """Screen batch of ligands"""
    results = []
    for ligand in ligands_batch:
        result = screen_ligand.delay(
            ligand["id"],
            ligand["smiles"],
            receptor_file
        )
        results.append(result)
    return [r.get() for r in results]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.start()' > /app/screening/scheduler.py \
    && chmod +x /app/screening/scheduler.py

# Create non-root user
RUN groupadd -r screener && useradd -r -g screener screener \
    && chown -R screener:screener /app

WORKDIR /app
USER screener

EXPOSE 6379 5555

CMD ["celery", "-A", "screening.scheduler", "worker", "--loglevel=info"]

Genetics
Chapter 7
Meiosis

7.1 Introduction

Meiosis is the process by whch diploid cells divide to form haploid gametes. It is a crucial step in sexual reproduction, allowing for genetic variation and diversity.

7.2 Meiotic Cell Division

Meiotic cell division is a two-part process consisting of meiosis I and meiosis II.

Meiosis I:

* Prophase I: Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange genetic material through crossing over.
* Metaphase I: Chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate.
* Anaphase I: Homologous chromosomes separate.
* Telophase I: Chromosomes reach the poles of the cell.

Meiosis II:

* Prophase II: Chromosomes condense and attach to the spindle fibers.
* Metaphase II: Chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate.
* Anaphase II: Sister chromatids separate.
* Telophase II: Chromosomes reach the poles of the cell.

7.3 Genetic Variation

Meiosis introduces genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

Data Processing
All concentrations reported as mean ± SD.
Calculations performed using spreadsheet software.

Removal Efficiency
Removal (%) = ((C0 − Ct) / C0) × 100.
C0: initial concentration.
Ct: concentration at time t.

First-Order Kinetics
ln(Ct/C0) = −k_obs t.
Plot ln(Ct/C0) versus time.
k_obs extracted from slope.

Pseudo-Second-Order
1/Ct = 1/C0 + k2 t.
Fit 1/Ct vs t.

Adsorption Isotherms
Langmuir model: Ce/qe = (1/(qmax KL)) + (Ce/qmax).
Freundlich: ln(qe) = ln(KF) + (1/n) ln(Ce).

Model Selection
Use adjusted R^2 and residual plots.

Statistical Tests
Two-tailed t-test for pairwise comparisons.
Significance threshold p < 0.05.

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

Example Calculation (Text Only)
C0 = 10.0 mg/L.
Ct = 2.5 mg/L at t = 60 min.
Removal (%) = ((10.0 − 2.5)/10.0) × 100 = 75%.

Kinetics Example
At t = 30 min, Ct = 6.0 mg/L.
Compute ln(6/10) = ln(0.6) = −0.5108.

Uncertainty Propagation
For ratio Ct/C0, relative uncertainty computed via standard error propagation.

Linearity assessed by R^2 > 0.999.

text:
Chaptr 1: The Fundamentals of Cell Biology

Cells are the basic unit of life. All organisms, from the simle bacteria to the complex human, are made up of cells. Each cell contains organelles that perform specific functions.

Mitochondria, known as the power houses of the cell, generate ATP through the process of cellular respiration. The cell's nucleus houses the genetic material, DNA.

Cell division is a critical process for growth and repair. Mitosis and meiosis are two types of cell division. Mitosis produces two identical daughter cells, while meiosis results in four genetically diverse gametes.

Errors in cell division can lead to diseases such as cancer. Understanding the cell cycle is vital for developing treatments.

Cell membranes are selectively permeable, allowing certain molecules to pass while excluding others. This property is crucial for maintaining homeostasis.

In multicellular organisms, cells specialize to perform distinct functions. This specialization is essential for the organism's survival.

Recent advances in microscopy have allowed scientists to study cells in greater detail. Techniques like fluorescence microscopy provide insights into cellular processes.

text:
Introduction to Genetics

Genetics is the study of heredity and variation in living organisms. Genes, which are segments of DNA, determine the traits of an organism.

Mendel's laws of inheritance laid the foundation for modern genetics. He discovered that traits are inherited in discrete units, now known as genes.

Dominant and recessive alleles determine the expression of traits. An organism inherits two alleles for each gene, one from each parent.

Mutations in genes can lead to genetic disorders. Some mutations are beneficial, while others are harmful.

Genetic engineering allows scientists to modify organisms' DNA. This technology has applications in medicine, agriculture, and industry.

Genomics, the study of an organism's entire genome, has revolutionized biology. It enables the identification of genes associated with diseases.

Epigenetics explores how gene expression is regulated without changing the DNA sequence. Environmental factors can influence epigenetic changes.

DNA replication is a critical process that occurs before cell division. It ensures that each daughter cell receives an identical copy of the DNA.

text:
Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert light energy into chemical energy. It occurs in the chloroplasts and involves the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

The equation for photosynthesis is: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

Cellular respiration is the process by which cells convert glucose into ATP. It occurs in the mitochondria and involves glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain.

The equation for cellular respiration is: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP.

Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are complementary processes. Photosynthesis produces oxygen and glucose, which are used in cellular respiration.

Plants, algae, and some bacteria perform photosynthesis. These organisms are known as autotrophs.

Heterotrophs, such as animals, rely on consuming autotrophs for energy.

Understanding these processes is crucial for studying ecosystems and energy flow.

text:
The Nervous System

The nervous system is responsible for coordinating an organism's response to its environment. It consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

The CNS includes the brain and spinal cord. It processes information and sends signals to the PNS.

The PNS consists of sensory and motor neurons. Sensory neurons transmit information from the body to the CNS, while motor neurons carry signals from the CNS to the muscles.

Neurons communicate through synapses. Neurotransmitters are released at synapses to transmit signals between neurons.

The brain is the control center of the nervous system. It regulates vital functions such as breathing, heart rate, and digestion.

The spinal cord acts as a conduit for signals between the brain and the body. It also coordinates reflexes.

The autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary functions such as heart rate and digestion. It has two divisions: the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.

text:
Ecology and Ecosystems

Ecology is the study of interactions between organisms and their environment. Ecosystems are communities of living organisms interacting with their physical environment.

Producers, consumers, and decomposers are the three main components of an ecosystem. Producers, such as plants, convert energy from the sun into food.

Consumers, such as animals, obtain energy by eating producers or other consumers. Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients.

Energy flow and nutrient cycling are critical processes in ecosystems. Energy flows from producers to consumers, while nutrients cycle through the ecosystem.

Biodiversity is the variety of life in an ecosystem. It is essential for ecosystem stability and resilience.

Human activities, such as deforestation and pollution, can disrupt ecosystems and reduce biodiversity.

Conservation efforts aim to protect ecosystems and preserve biodiversity.

text:
Evolutionary Biology

Evolution is the process by which species change over time. It is driven by mechanisms such as natural selection, genetic drift, and gene flow.

Natural selection occurs when individuals with advantageous traits are more likely to survive and reproduce. These traits become more common in the population over time.

Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies in a population. It can lead to the loss of genetic variation.

Gene flow is the transfer of genetic material between populations. It can introduce new genetic variation.

Speciation is the formation of new species. It occurs when populations become reproductively isolated.

The fossil record provides evidence for evolution. It shows the gradual changes in species over time.

Molecular biology techniques, such as DNA sequencing, have provided insights into evolutionary relationships.

Understanding evolution is crucial for fields such as medicine and conservation biology.

text:
Plant Biology

Plants are multicellular organisms that perform photosynthesis. They are essential for life on Earth, as they produce oxygen and food.

Plants have several key structures: roots, stems, leaves, and flowers. Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and nutrients. Stems support the plant and transport materials. Leaves are the primary sites of photosynthesis. Flowers are involved in reproduction.

Plant hormones regulate growth and development. Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene, and abscisic acid are the main plant hormones.

Plants have various adaptations to survive in different environments. Xerophytes, such as cacti, are adapted to arid conditions. Hydrophytes, such as water lilies, are adapted to aquatic environments.

Tropisms are directional growth responses to environmental stimuli. Phototropism is growth towards light, while gravitropism is growth in response to gravity.

Understanding plant biology is crucial for agriculture and food production.

text:
Animal Physiology

Animal physiology is the study of how animals' bodies function. It includes the study of systems such as the circulatory, respiratory, nervous, and digestive systems.

The circulatory system transports nutrients, gases, and wastes throughout the body. The heart pumps blood, which carries these substances.

The respiratory system facilitates gas exchange. Oxygen is taken in from the environment, and carbon dioxide is expelled.

The nervous system coordinates the body's responses to internal and external stimuli. It includes the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.

The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients that can be absorbed and used by the body.

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment. It is essential for the proper functioning of physiological processes.

Hormones regulate various physiological processes. They are chemical messengers that travel through the bloodstream.

text:
Microbiology

Microbiology is the study of microorganisms, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa. These organisms are often too small to be seen with the naked eye.

Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes. They can be beneficial, such as those in the human gut, or pathogenic, causing diseases.

Viruses are acellular entities that require a host cell to replicate. They can cause a wide range of diseases, from the common cold to AIDS.

Fungi can be unicellular, like yeasts, or multicellular, like molds. They play a crucial role in decomposition and nutrient cycling.

Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes. Some are free-living, while others are parasitic.

Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections. However, the overuse of antibiotics has led to the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Vaccines are used to prevent viral infections. They stimulate the immune system to recognize and fight specific viruses.

Microbiology has important applications in medicine, agriculture, and industry.

text:
Developmental Biology

Developmental biology is the study of how organisms grow and develop from a single cell into a complex, multicellular organism. It involves the study of processes such as cell division, differentiation, and morphogenesis.

During development, cells divide and differentiate into various cell types. This process is regulated by genes and signaling pathways.

Morphogenesis is the process by which the organism takes shape. It involves the coordinated movement and organization of cells.

Embryonic development begins with fertilization, the fusion of a sperm and egg cell. The resulting zygote undergoes rapid cell division and forms a blastula.

Gastrulation is the process by which the blastula forms three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. These layers give rise to all the tissues and organs of the organism.

Induction is the process by which one group of cells influences the development of another group. It is essential for proper organ formation.

Understanding developmental biology is crucial for fields such as regenerative medicine and stem cell research.

text: The global mean temperature has been rising steadily over the past century, with a significant increase observed in the last few decades. The primary causes are attributed to the enhanced greenhouse effect resulting from increased concentrations of CO2 and other greenhouse gases. This trend is expected to continue if current emission patterns persist.

text:
Transcription factors are proteins that regulate gene expression by binding to DNA. The following discussion explores their mechanisms and types.

Key Mechanisms:
• DNA Binding Domain - This protein segment allows transcription factors to recognize specific DNA sequences, often through helix-turn-helix structures or zinc fingers.
• Activation Domain - Mediates interactions with coactivator proteins to recruit RNA polymerase II, involving intrinsically disordered regions that undergo phase separation in nuclear compartments.
• Dimerization Motifs - Many factors form homo- or heterodimers, expanding regulatory capacity through combinations like basic helix-loop-helix dimers.

Classification:
1. Based on structural domains: Homeodomain, Leucine zipper, and HMG-box containing proteins show distinct evolutionary adaptations in DNA binding specificity.
2. By regulatory function: Activators enhance transcription rates, while repressors can silence genes through chromatin remodeling complexes such as Polycomb group proteins.
3. Temporal expression: Pioneering transcription factors in development initiate cascades, whereas housekeeping factors maintain constitutive expression.

Case Study - HNF4α in Liver Development:
This nuclear receptor coordinates hepatocyte differentiation by occupying enhancers in embryonic stem cells. Its loss leads to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, demonstrating essential roles in metabolic homeostasis maintenance.

Challenges in Study:
Single-cell omics reveal heterogeneity in factor expression across cell types, requiring computational models to predict cooperativity effects and binding site selection across the genome.

Introduction
Coastal ecosystems exemplify the interplay between abiotic factors and biological diversity. This analysis focuses on trophic relationships and anthropogenic impacts.

Case Study 1: Coral Reef Regime Shift
When herbivorous fish populations decline, macroalgae dominate coral through allelopathic inhibition. Experimental caging studies show recovery potential when parrotfish biomass remains >200g/m².

Case Study 2: Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vents
Chemotrophic bacteria form the base of food webs, fixing carbon through reverse Krebs cycles. Vent fauna exhibit convergent evolutionary adaptations like hemocyanin with pressure-stable oxygen binding.

Stressor Impacts:
Physical Damage: Undersea mining destroys habitat-forming sponges that take decades to regrow
Chemical Pollution: Organotins bioaccumulate, causing imposex in gastropods through endocrine disruption
Temperature Effects: Thermal stress dissociates coral-algal symbiosis, with molecular chaperones failing to prevent protein denaturation

Ecosystem Monitoring Challenges
Current methods combine remote sensing (chlorophyll a concentrations) with eDNA sampling, though temporal scales mismatch between satellite data and microbial community lag responses.

Fresh samples immersed in FAA solution (37% formaldehyde: glacial acetic acid: ethanol, 5:0.5:95 ratio) preserves tissue structure for sectioning.

4. Dehydrate through ethanol series before mounting

Observations:
Species A shows 3.5µm thick cuticle layers with epicuticular waxes forming crystalline deposits. Vascular bundles exhibit C4-type kranz anatomy with distinct bundle sheath cells containing 15-20 chloroplasts. Stomatal complexes possess three subsidiary cells arranged in a triangular pattern

Discussion
These adaptations align with the Opuntia clade's evolutionary radiation under arid conditions, suggesting co-regulation of stomatal development genes like EPF1 and wax biosynthesis pathways involving CER6 orthologs.

Protein Folding Dynamics in ER Chaperones

Chapter Overview
This analysis examines calnexin's role in glycoprotein maturation within the endoplasmic reticulum. The process involves multiple coordinated steps:

1. Monoglucosylation
- The GT enzyme adds glucose residues to partially folded proteins
- The UDP-glucose regenerating system maintains energy efficiency
- Timing of glucose removal determines progression to quality control

2. Fold Assistance Mechanisms
Calnexin forms transient complexes with ATP-regulated lid structures. The negatively charged cavity allows selective substrate binding, with acidic residues stabilizing hydrophobic exposed regions during folding intermediates.

3. Release Control
PDI-family oxidoreductases catalyze disulfide bond formation. Protein dithiol isomerase creates correct disulfide pairings through two catalytically active thioredoxin domains with specific substrate recognition motifs.

4. Exit Decisions
Misfolded proteins trigger the UPR pathway via IRE1α oligomerization. PERK-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation reduces global translation while increasing ATF4 levels for chaperone gene expression.

Experimental Findings
Fluorescence recovery assays show calnexin-bound intermediates reside in ER exit sites for 8-12 minutes before anterograde transport in COPII vesicles containing Sec24D cargo adaptors.

The Human Genome Project: Scientific Legacy

Initial Objectives (1990):
1. Sequence all 3.2 billion base pairs in human DNA
2. Identify all approximately 20,000 protein-coding genes
3. Develop computational tools for sequence analysis
4. Address ethical implications of genetic data

Technological Innovations:
• BAC cloning enabled accurate assembly of repetitive sequences longer than 150kb through overlapping fingerprints
• Capillary sequencers revolutionized throughput, reading 500 bases per hour compared to slab gel's 100 bases every two hours
• Assembly algorithms (e.g., Celera Genomics' ARACHNE) improved gap resolution in heterochromatic regions

Post-Project Discoveries:
2005 Findings:
- ENCODE project showed 76% of DNA undergoes non-coding transcription, challenging traditional gene-centric views
- Copy number variation accounts for 12% of genetic differences between individuals, exceeding single nucleotide polymorphisms' contribution
- Pseudogenes maintain 78% sequence identity on average with functional paralogs, suggesting widespread gene conversion activity

Contemporary Applications:
- Precision medicine initiatives use SNP arrays to calculate polygenic risk scores with 83% accuracy for type 2 diabetes prediction
- Gene editing employs T cell receptor modification in 63% of CAR-T cancer therapies, directly stemming from genome project data
- Microbiome studies leverage 16S rRNA sequencing to link gut microbial gene counts (150-fold expansion over human genome) with metabolic diseases

Cellular Respiration: Energetic Transitions Through Metabolism

Glycolysis Overview:
This conserved pathway converts glucose to pyruvate through 10 enzymatic steps. Key regulatory points involve:
1. Hexokinase: Phosphorylates glucose with 0.1μM KM, showing negative cooperativity
2. Phosphofructokinase: Allosteric regulation by ATP at inhibitory sites (K0.5 30μM), while AMP enhances activity at activator sites
3. Pyruvate Kinase: Hormones control its phosphenolpyruvate carboxykinase-mediated regulation in liver cells

Transition Reaction:
In mitochondrial matrix, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes decarboxylation through three enzyme subunits:
• E1 decarboxylates pyruvate with TPP cofactor
• E2 transfers acetyl-TPP to lipoamide
• E3 regenerates oxidized lipoamide using FAD prosthetic groups
This complex requires five vitamins: thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, pantothenic acid, and lipoic acid as coenzyme precursors

Citric Acid Cycle Dynamics:
Aconitase facilitates isomerization by rearranging hydroxyl groups through an iron-sulfur active site. The enzyme's Fe-S cluster binds citrate in two distinct orientations before releasing isocitrate with 34% stereochemical inversion

Electron Transport Chain:
Complex V (ATP synthase) contains the proton-driven rotor with 14 c-subunits. Each rotation produces 3 ATPs through the binding change mechanism, where β-subunits cycle through loose, tight, and open conformations synchronizing with proton translocation.

Evolution of Antibiotic Resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae

Background
Emerging serotype 19A strains exhibit multidrug resistance, challenging community-acquired pneumonia treatment paradigms. This case study combines genomic and clinical data.

Genomic Analysis
Whole-genome sequencing revealed 23 genetic elements acquired through horizontal transfer, including:
- TetM-mediated tetracycline resistance integrated with transposon Tn916
- ermB gene conferring macrolide resistance, associated with conjugative transposon CTnSp_1
- β-lactamase operon acquired from oral streptococcal donors

Mechanism Evolution
Capsular switch events involved:
1. Recombination between serotype 19F and 15B isolates at the cps locus
2. Point mutations in wzy gene creating novel polysaccharide linkages
3. Loss of phase-variable DNA methyltransferase (SspI) expression increasing recombination frequency

Spread Dynamics
Epidemiological modeling shows basic reproductive number R0 = 3.6 in daycare settings, with 62% of transmissions occurring before symptom onset. Resistance persistence involves:
- Bacteriophage-induced lysis releasing plasmids for transformation
- Competence-stimulating peptide variants enhancing DNA uptake
- Biofilm-associated persister cell formation protecting subpopulations

Treatment Challenges
Fluoroquinolone resistance develops through S81F ParC mutations requiring two nucleotide substitutions. This genetic barrier explains its slower resistance emergence compared to single mutation mechanisms like mecA in staphylococci.

text:
Neurotransmitter Systems: Comparative Analysis

Major Excitatory Systems:
1. Glutamatergic
- Synthesizes from glutamine via glutaminase in synaptic vesicles (VACV compartment)
- NMDA receptors contain NR2B subunit dominant in adolescent brains, with slower deactivation kinetics than adult NR2A
- AMPA receptor desensitization prevents overexcitation through TARP stoichiometry modulation

2. Cholinergic
Basal forebrain neurons synthesize acetylcholine using vesicular transporter VAChT that operates at pH 5.5 with KM 8μM. Receptor subtypes:
- M1 mAChR couples to Gq proteins for PLC activation in hippocampal pyramidal cells
- α4β2 nAChR in locus coeruleus exhibits high conductance states (40pS), influencing noradrenergic release

Major Inhibitory Systems:
1. GABAergic
- GAD65 and GAD67 isoforms synthesize GABA through decarboxylation
- GABA-T enzyme converts GABA to succinic semialdehyde in presynaptic terminals
- Benzodiazepines bind at α+/γ2− interfaces of GABAA receptor complexes

2. Glycinergic
Glycine transporters (GlyT1/2) show different affinities - GlyT1 maintains synaptic concentration (<1μM) while GlyT2 packages vesicles with 300:1 uptake ratio
